Let the policy office edit the live prompt directly and keep a dated log of each change that was made and by whom
Freeze the prompt after launch so the behaviour that passed acceptance testing can never change
Require the policy owner's approval and a passing eval-suite run before any prompt change is released
questions.explain: Prompts are production code: versioning makes changes attributable and reversible, and owner approval plus an eval run gates a change before citizens see it, so the policy office can iterate safely. Direct edits with a log are the near-miss: the log gives traceability, but it is an after-the-fact record and a bad edit reaches citizens before anyone tests it. Freezing blocks the iteration the policy office needs.
questions.constraint: a bad wording change reaches citizens immediately; policy office owns content
breaks: a log records a bad edit after citizens have already seen it
blocks the iteration the policy office needs

questions.q: A contractor will build the agency's integration from your design. Which documentation best guides the implementation?
options: A slide deck summarising the vision, the benefits and the high-level system diagram
The full prompt text alone, since the prompt is where all of the system's logic lives
Decision records with rejected options, interface contracts and the eval acceptance bar
A list of the vendor features used, linked to the vendor's public documentation pages
questions.explain: Implementers need to know what to build (interface contracts), why it is built that way (decision records, including rejected alternatives so they are not reopened), and how done is judged (eval acceptance criteria). The slide deck is the near-miss: it aligns people on the vision, but gives the builder no contracts or acceptance bar. The prompt is only one component, and vendor feature links describe the platform, not this design.
questions.constraint: a contractor builds the integration from the design
breaks: a slide deck gives no contracts or acceptance bar
the prompt is only one component
vendor links describe the platform, not this design

questions.q: About 45% of conversations are 'where is my order?', answered from a single tracking lookup. Which approach fits that slice of traffic best?
options: Route it to a fixed path: one tracking lookup, then a short reply from a small model
Send it through the full support agent with every tool, like every other conversation type
Answer it with a large model and extended thinking so delivery estimates are well reasoned
Hand it to human agents, since order status questions are too important to automate at all
questions.explain: A known, single-step intent needs the least complex pattern: classify, run the one lookup, and have a small fast model phrase the answer. The full agent is the near-miss: it would answer correctly, but pays agent-level tokens and latency on almost half of all traffic for a path that never varies. Extended thinking adds cost for no reasoning gain, and sending the highest-volume, simplest intent to humans defeats the business case.
questions.constraint: 45% of traffic is one tracking lookup
breaks: agent cost and latency on a path that never varies
extended thinking adds cost for no reasoning gain
humans on the highest-volume, simplest intent defeat the business case

questions.q: The CFO will compare the assistant against the $4 cost of a human-handled contact. Which measure should the business case use?
options: Model spend per conversation, compared directly with the $4 cost of a human contact
The share of conversations that end without a human, whether or not they were resolved
Total cost per resolved issue, counting escalations and repeat contacts in 7 days
Tokens per conversation, tracked weekly to show that the prompt is getting more efficient
questions.explain: The fair comparison is cost per issue actually resolved: an AI conversation that escalates, or brings the customer back two days later, carries those costs too. Model spend per conversation is the near-miss: it is the obvious unit, but it ignores the human cost of escalations and repeat contacts, so it flatters the assistant. Containment without resolution rewards conversations that end badly, and tokens per conversation is an engineering metric, not a business case.
questions.constraint: the CFO compares against a $4 human-handled contact
breaks: ignores the human cost of escalations and repeat contacts
containment without resolution rewards conversations that end badly
tokens per conversation is an engineering metric, not a business case

questions.q: A customer's one message raises problems with three separate orders. The first reply must arrive inside the 3-second SLA, the customer should see one coherent answer, and each lookup is a simple read of a single order that must reflect its status at the moment of the call. Which orchestration fits?
options: Spawn three subagents, each given the full conversation and every available tool, then merge their three replies into one answer
Handle the orders one after another across three turns, confirming each one with the customer as it goes
Issue the three order lookups as parallel tool calls in one turn, then write a single reply from the results
Use a larger model with extended thinking so one long, careful response covers all three orders at once
questions.explain: Independent simple reads inside a 3-second SLA call for parallel tool calls in one turn and a single model call to write the reply. Three subagents is the near-miss: it parallelises, but each re-reads the whole conversation and the merge adds a step, spending the latency budget on overhead. Sequential turns triple the wait, and a larger model with extended thinking adds latency to lookups that need no deeper reasoning.
questions.constraint: 3-second first-reply SLA, one coherent reply, three independent simple lookups
breaks: multi-agent overhead and a merge step eat the 3-second budget
triples the waiting and breaks the single coherent reply
a bigger model adds latency to independent reads that need no deeper reasoning

questions.q: The system prompt has grown to 30,000 tokens of return rules for 14 product categories, and the agent sometimes applies the wrong category's rule. What change fits best?
options: Keep a short core prompt and load only the relevant category's rules once it is identified
Cache the full 30,000-token prompt so the cost of carrying all 14 rule sets drops sharply
Put the 14 category rule sets under bold headings so the model can find the right one faster
Move to the model with the largest context window so all 14 rule sets fit more comfortably
questions.explain: The error comes from 13 irrelevant rule sets competing with the right one. Modular prompts that load only the identified category's rules remove the confusion and cut tokens. Caching is the near-miss: it is a sound optimisation for a large static prefix and would cut cost, but every rule set is still in the context, so the wrong-rule errors remain. Bold headings are cosmetic, and a bigger window holds the same noise.
questions.constraint: 30,000-token prompt; the wrong category's rule gets applied
breaks: caching cuts cost but every rule set stays in context and the errors remain
bold headings are cosmetic
a bigger window holds the same noise

questions.q: The team added step-by-step reasoning to every reply. Latency rose 40%, quality on simple intents stayed flat, and dispute handling improved. What should they do?
options: Keep step-by-step reasoning on every reply, since better reasoning is worth the latency
Use reasoning only on complex intents such as disputes, and drop it from simple intents
Keep reasoning on every reply but hide it from the customer so that it feels much faster
Remove reasoning everywhere and add more few-shot examples to make up for the quality loss
questions.explain: Chain-of-thought pays off where the task needs reasoning, so apply it per intent: disputes keep it, simple intents drop it and get their speed back. Hiding the reasoning is the near-miss: it tidies the display, but the tokens are still generated, so the latency and cost remain. Reasoning everywhere wastes latency on simple intents, and removing it everywhere gives up the measured dispute gains.
questions.constraint: reasoning raised latency 40% and helps only disputes
breaks: pays 40% latency on simple intents with no quality gain
hidden reasoning tokens still cost the same latency
gives up the measured dispute gains

questions.q: The support assistant sometimes tells customers 'it will arrive tomorrow' when tracking data shows no such date. A wrongly promised date triggers refund claims, so the fix must be enforced by the system rather than hoped for. Which TWO changes address it most reliably? Select TWO.
options: Tell the model in the system prompt to be extremely careful and conservative about making any promises to customers about delivery
Restrict delivery dates in replies to values returned by the tracking tool in the same conversation
Add an output check that compares every date in the reply with the tracking data and blocks mismatches
Move to a larger model, since smaller models tend to overpromise in order to please customers and larger ones do so less
questions.explain: The constraint is enforcement: ground dates in the tracking tool, then verify what is actually in the reply against the same data, which catches any phrasing. The prompt caution is the near-miss: it points in the right direction and is cheap, but a prompt shapes behaviour without enforcing it, so a promise can still slip out. A larger model does not ground a date in data it was never given.
questions.constraint: wrong promises cost refunds, so the fix must be enforced, not hoped for
breaks: a firmer prompt shapes behaviour but does not enforce it
model size does not ground a date in tracking data

questions.q: Running a reranked knowledge-base lookup on every conversation pushed p95 first response from 2.8 to 4.5 seconds against a 3-second SLA. Only about 3% of conversations are policy questions that need the lookup, and policy answers must stay as accurate as they are now. Which configuration decision is easiest to justify?
options: Drop the reranker for every intent and accept lower answer quality to bring latency back under three seconds
Raise the SLA to five seconds for all conversations because accuracy matters more than speed in support
Pre-generate answers to the 500 most common questions and never call the model for those questions
Run the reranked lookup only for intents that need policy text, and skip it for order-status conversations
questions.explain: Two constraints compete: a 3-second SLA and unchanged policy accuracy. Spending latency only where it buys accuracy satisfies both, since 97% of traffic never pays for the lookup, so p95 falls back near the old 2.8 seconds. Dropping the reranker is the near-miss: it does cut latency, but it lowers quality for exactly the policy answers the lookup was added for. Moving the SLA abandons a commitment, and canned answers go stale as policies and order details change.
questions.constraint: 3-second SLA, and policy answers must stay as accurate as now
breaks: lowers accuracy for the policy answers the lookup exists to protect
abandons the committed 3-second SLA
canned answers go stale and cannot reflect order or policy changes

questions.q: Model spend doubled overnight while traffic stayed flat. Which telemetry would find the cause fastest?
options: The provider's monthly invoice by model, compared with the invoice from last month
A count of conversations per hour, compared with the same hour on the previous day
Per-request tokens and tool-call counts by intent and prompt version over time
The day's customer satisfaction scores, to see whether the extra spend helped anyone
questions.explain: Per-request token and tool-call telemetry, tagged by intent and prompt version, shows at once which slice changed and when, for example a new prompt version causing repeated tool calls. The monthly invoice is the near-miss: it is the authoritative cost figure, but it is weeks late and too coarse to point at a cause. Conversation counts confirm traffic is flat but not why, and satisfaction scores do not explain spend.
questions.constraint: spend doubled overnight while traffic stayed flat
breaks: the monthly invoice is weeks late and too coarse
a conversation count confirms flat traffic but not why
satisfaction scores do not explain spend

questions.q: An A/B test shows a new prompt lifts the resolution rate by 3 points, but repeat contacts within seven days also rise by 4 points. Both differences are statistically significant and the test ran its planned length. What should the team conclude?
options: Ship it, since the resolution rate is the primary metric and it rose by three points
Run the test again for twice as long to be sure the three-point gain is not noise
Judge on resolved-without-repeat-contact, the metric that reflects true resolution
Ship it only to customers who have never contacted support, to limit the impact
questions.explain: Repeat contacts are the guardrail that exposes false resolutions: the new prompt appears to close conversations sooner without solving the problem, so the decision should rest on resolution without a repeat contact, which this result suggests got worse. Rerunning the test is the near-miss: more data is right when a result is marginal, but both differences are already significant over the planned run, and a longer run will not fix a misleading primary metric. Shipping on the headline number ignores the guardrail, and a narrower rollout still ships the regression.
questions.constraint: both differences significant over the planned run; repeat contacts rose
breaks: ignores the repeat-contact guardrail
a longer run will not fix a misleading primary metric
a narrower rollout still ships the regression

questions.q: The resolution rate has plateaued at 71% for two months. Which improvement process is most likely to raise it?
options: Try a new prompt wording each week and keep whichever week had the best resolution rate
Cluster failed conversations by cause, fix the biggest cluster, add its cases to evals
Upgrade to the newest model whenever one is released, and measure the change afterwards
Survey customers about which features they would like the support assistant to add next
questions.explain: Iterative improvement works from evidence: group failures by root cause, fix the biggest group, and lock the fix in with regression cases so it does not come back. Weekly prompt trials are the near-miss: they do iterate, but week-to-week traffic differences swamp the effect, and nothing ties a change to a failure cause. Model upgrades are not a diagnosis, and feature wishes do not explain current failures.
questions.constraint: resolution plateaued at 71% for two months
breaks: week-to-week traffic differences swamp the effect
an upgrade is not a diagnosis
feature wishes do not explain current failures

questions.q: To save cost the team moved to a smaller model. Simple returns still work, but multi-step exchanges (swap a size, then refund the price difference) now fail often. The prompt and tools are unchanged, and most of the saving should be kept. What is the most likely diagnosis and fix?
options: The smaller model is a mismatch for multi-step intents; route those intents up a tier and keep the rest on the small model
The prompt is unclear, so add much more detailed instructions for exchanges, size swaps and partial refunds before each call
The tools are failing, so add retries around the exchange and refund tool calls in the agent
The context is too long, so trim the conversation history on every request before it is sent to the smaller model
questions.explain: Failures began with the model change and appear only on multi-step cases, which points to a model mismatch for that complexity; routing only those intents up keeps most of the saving. The more detailed prompt is the near-miss: clearer instructions can sometimes rescue a weaker model, but the prompt did not change and worked before the swap, so it is not the cause. Nothing suggests tool errors, and conversation history length did not change with the model swap.
questions.constraint: only the model changed; failures are limited to multi-step intents; keep most of the saving
breaks: the prompt did not change and worked before the model swap, so it is not the layer at fault
the tools did not change and failures began only with the model swap
history length was not the change

questions.q: Which TWO changes cut model spend the most with the least effect on customer experience? Select TWO.
options: Cache the static system prompt and tool definitions shared by every conversation
Send live customer replies through the Batches API to get the lower batch price
Move the nightly conversation-summary job for QA review onto the Batches API
Cap every reply at 50 output tokens so that no response can run up the token bill
questions.explain: Caching cuts the cost of the identical prefix on every request without changing a single answer, and the nightly summary job is not interactive, so batch pricing costs it nothing in experience. Batching live replies is the near-miss: the discount is real, but batch results can take hours, which is unacceptable in a live chat. A 50-token cap truncates answers customers need.
questions.constraint: cut spend with the least effect on customer experience
breaks: batch results can take hours, unacceptable in live chat
a 50-token cap truncates answers customers need

questions.q: The assistant will start reading customer-written product reviews to answer product questions. Which risk is introduced specifically by that change?
options: Reviews are often negative, so the main risk is that the agent becomes less polite
Reviews add tokens, so the main risk is that cost per conversation will rise sharply
Reviews may contain instructions the agent follows, so treat them as untrusted data
Reviews may be outdated, so the main risk is that the agent quotes an old price
questions.explain: Any third-party text the model reads can carry indirect prompt injection, so reviews must be handled as untrusted data, kept out of instruction positions and away from tools they could trigger. Outdated content is the near-miss: staleness is a real quality issue, but prices come from the catalogue, and staleness is not the new security risk that untrusted text brings. Token cost is manageable, and negative tone does not change the agent's own instructions.
questions.constraint: new risk from reading customer-written reviews
breaks: tone does not change the agent's instructions
token cost is manageable and not a new risk
staleness is a quality issue, not the new security risk

questions.q: Peak season brings about four times normal traffic. The support VP wants to know in advance what to expect, and the API has rate limits that cannot be raised instantly. The VP will be held to whatever is promised to customers during the peak. How should you set expectations before the peak?
options: Promise the normal SLA through the peak, since the API scales automatically with demand and capacity is no concern
Agree peak SLA targets and a written degradation plan, with triggers such as a fallback model or human queue
Tell the VP that peak performance cannot be predicted, so no targets can be agreed in advance of the season
Ask the VP to cap marketing campaigns and promotions during peak so that traffic stays close to normal levels
questions.explain: Expectation alignment means agreeing in advance what good looks like under four times load and what happens when limits are reached, with clear triggers. Promising the normal SLA is the near-miss: capacity can be planned, but rate limits are not raised instantly, so an unconditional promise is untested. Refusing to set targets avoids the planning, and asking the business to cap demand moves the problem without solving it.
questions.constraint: four times normal traffic; rate limits cannot be raised instantly
breaks: an unconditional promise that rate limits cannot back
avoids the planning the VP asked for
moves the problem to the business instead of planning for the demand

questions.q: Human support agents fear the assistant will replace them, and the escalation notes they write have become terse, hurting handoffs. What is the best response?
options: Explain to the agents that leadership has decided and the rollout schedule will not change
Add a rule requiring escalation notes to reach a minimum length before they can be saved
Replace the human escalation path with a second model so the agents' notes no longer matter
Involve agents in labelling evals and reviewing handoffs, and show how their role shifts
questions.explain: Adoption depends on the people around the system: involving agents in evaluation and handoff design uses their expertise, gives them a stake in the outcome, and makes the role change concrete. The minimum-length rule is the near-miss: it targets the visible symptom, but it produces padded notes without addressing why people disengaged. Announcing the decision hardens resistance, and removing humans from escalation removes the safety net.
questions.constraint: agents fear replacement and their escalation notes got terse
breaks: announcing the decision hardens resistance
a minimum length produces padded notes, not engagement
removes the human safety net

questions.q: Security requires that no engineer's Claude Code can read .env files or run certain deploy commands, and that nobody can override this locally. 600 engineers work across 40 teams' repositories, and new repos appear weekly. Which TWO settings fit? Select TWO.
options: Deploy managed policy settings from IT to every machine, so user and project settings cannot loosen them
Express the rules as permission deny rules for .env reads and the deploy commands, which the tool enforces
A deny rule in each repo's committed .claude/settings.json, added and maintained by every team lead for their repo
A rule in each repo's CLAUDE.md telling Claude never to read secrets or run those commands
questions.explain: Both constraints, no local override and coverage of new repos, point to managed policy at the top of the settings hierarchy, and the rules themselves should be deny rules that the tool enforces, not wording the model may follow. Per-repo deny rules are the near-miss: the mechanism is right, but they depend on 40 leads adding them, can be edited by any committer and miss new repos. CLAUDE.md is guidance to the model, not enforcement.
questions.constraint: no local override, 40 teams, new repos weekly
breaks: editable by any committer and absent from new repos until a lead adds it
guidance to the model, not enforcement

questions.q: Each team wants its coding standards applied for every engineer working in its repo, while engineers keep their personal preferences. Where should each live?
options: Both in managed policy settings, so the platform team controls every engineer's preferences
Team standards in each engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md; personal ones in the repo CLAUDE.md
Team standards in the committed repo CLAUDE.md; personal ones in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Both in the committed repo CLAUDE.md, with each engineer's preferences under a heading
questions.explain: Project memory committed in the repo is shared by everyone who works there; user memory in the home directory applies only to that engineer across projects. Putting both in the repo file is the near-miss: the team part is right, but personal preferences then load for every teammate and turn the shared file into a list of individual quirks. Swapping the two locations inverts sharing, and managed policy is for organisation rules, not personal style.
questions.constraint: team standards must be shared; personal preferences must stay personal
breaks: managed policy is for organisation rules, not personal style
inverts sharing: team standards stay private to one engineer
personal preferences would load for every teammate

questions.q: Teams want the internal Jira and docs MCP servers available automatically in their repos. Each engineer has a personal API token that must never be committed to git, and new joiners should work without a setup checklist. How should the servers be configured?
options: Commit a project .mcp.json with one shared service token written directly into the file
Have each engineer add the servers by hand in user scope, following a wiki setup checklist
Commit a project .mcp.json that reads each engineer's token from an environment variable
Paste the internal APIs' documentation into CLAUDE.md so that Claude can call those APIs directly
questions.explain: A committed project-scope .mcp.json gives everyone the same servers on checkout, and environment-variable expansion keeps each engineer's credential out of git. The shared token in the file is the near-miss: same mechanism, but it commits a secret and makes every action look like one account. Manual user-scope setup needs the very checklist the team wants to avoid and drifts, and API documentation in CLAUDE.md is not an integration.
questions.constraint: token must never be committed; new joiners work without a checklist
breaks: commits a secret to git and makes every action look like one account
needs the setup checklist the team wants to avoid and drifts
documentation is not an integration and carries no authentication

questions.q: Twelve teams each wrote their own long prompt for the same database-migration checklist, and the copies have drifted apart. What is the best way to share one version?
options: Paste the agreed checklist into every repo's CLAUDE.md so it loads in each session
Email the agreed checklist to every team and ask them to replace their own copies
Package it as one versioned Skill in an internal plugin that teams install
Let each team keep its own version, since every team knows its own databases best
questions.explain: A Skill in a shared plugin gives one owned, versioned source that updates everywhere, and only its short description loads until a migration task needs the full checklist. CLAUDE.md is the near-miss: it does share instructions, but the checklist would load in every session whether needed or not, and twelve pasted copies drift again. Email copies drift too, and separate versions keep the problem.
questions.constraint: twelve teams hold drifted copies of one checklist
breaks: loads in every session whether needed or not, and copies drift again
emailed copies drift too
separate versions keep the drift

questions.q: Human review of pull requests has become the bottleneck after the rollout. Which workflow change improves throughput while keeping quality control?
options: Run Claude in CI to post first-pass review comments, with humans keeping final approval
Let Claude approve and merge any PR that passes its own review, skipping human review
Have Claude rewrite each PR description so that human reviewers can skim it more quickly
Ask engineers to paste their diffs into a chat session before they request human review
questions.explain: An automated first pass in CI catches routine issues before a human looks, so reviewers spend their time on design and risk, while approval stays human. Auto-merge is the near-miss: it removes the bottleneck, but by removing the quality control too. Rewritten descriptions do not review code, and manual chat pastes are inconsistent and invisible to the team.
questions.constraint: review is the bottleneck; quality control must stay
breaks: removes the quality control along with the bottleneck
descriptions do not review code
manual pastes are inconsistent and invisible to the team

questions.q: Claude Code sessions in the monorepo hit context limits early. The root CLAUDE.md is 4,000 lines long and holds every team's full runbook. What is the best fix?
options: Ask engineers to run /compact more often so sessions recover space once they fill up
Trim the root file to shared essentials and move team detail to on-demand locations
Move the whole 4,000-line file into user scope so it loads from each home directory
Switch everyone to a model with a larger context window so the file fits comfortably
questions.explain: The root CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so it should hold only what everyone needs; team detail belongs in subdirectory CLAUDE.md files or Skills that load when relevant. Compacting more often is the near-miss: it frees space within a session, but treats the symptom while 4,000 lines reload into every new session. User scope still loads the same text for every engineer, and a bigger window keeps paying for it.
questions.constraint: a 4,000-line root CLAUDE.md loads in every session
breaks: compaction treats the symptom while the file reloads each session
user scope loads the same text for every engineer
a bigger window keeps paying for the file

questions.q: The CI job that runs Claude Code to review pull requests keeps failing: its tools need permission approval and nobody is there to give it. The job reads pull-request content from external contributors, and the repository also holds deploy credentials. Which TWO changes are right? Select TWO.
options: Run CI with all permission checks bypassed, since nobody is there to approve them anyway
Add retries so the job repeats the same tool calls each time one of them fails
Pre-approve only the specific tools the review needs, such as reading files and posting comments, in the CI run's permission settings
Run the job with a token limited to reading code and commenting on pull requests, with no deploy credentials
questions.explain: Headless runs need permissions decided in advance, so allow exactly the tools the review needs, and because the input is untrusted, limit the credentials the runner holds. Bypassing all checks is the near-miss: it stops the failures, but a prompt injection in an external PR would then have unrestricted tool access. Retries repeat the same denied calls.
questions.constraint: nobody to approve prompts, and the input is untrusted external pull requests
breaks: gives injected PR content unrestricted tool access on the runner
repeats the same denied calls

questions.q: The platform team must upgrade a deprecated logging library across 300 repositories owned by 40 teams. The change is the same everywhere, each owning team must review what lands in its repo, and the work should finish this week. Which TWO design choices fit? Select TWO.
options: Script a headless Claude Code run per repository, executed in parallel so each repo gets a fresh context
Ask each of the 40 teams to run the upgrade interactively in Claude Code on its own repositories, using a shared guide
Open each result as a pull request that the owning team reviews, rather than pushing to the default branch
Run one interactive session that clones all 300 repositories and edits them inside a single context
questions.explain: A repeated, well-defined change suits scripted headless runs, one per repo, in parallel, and the owning-team review constraint is met by landing each result as a pull request. Asking 40 teams to run it interactively is the near-miss: it keeps ownership, but multiplies effort by 40, makes progress hard to track and will not finish this week. One session over 300 repos overflows its context and gives no per-repo review point.
questions.constraint: same change in 300 repos, owning teams review, done this week
breaks: multiplies effort across 40 teams, cannot finish this week and progress is untracked
one context overflows across 300 repos and offers no per-repo review

questions.q: An internal platform-admin MCP server, with tools that can delete clusters, is in the shared configuration for all 600 engineers. Only on-call engineers ever need it. What should change?
options: Remove it from the shared config and enable it only for the on-call engineers
Keep it for everyone but have Claude confirm before any destructive tool call runs
Keep it for everyone and log every call so that misuse can be traced back afterwards
Rename its destructive tools with a 'danger_' prefix so that Claude avoids them lightly
questions.explain: Least privilege removes a capability from everyone who does not need it, which eliminates the risk rather than watching it. Confirmation is the near-miss: it adds a guard, but leaves cluster-deletion one approved prompt away for 600 people, most of whom have no reason to have it. Logging only detects misuse, and a name prefix is a hint, not a control.
questions.constraint: only on-call engineers need cluster-deleting tools
breaks: confirmation leaves deletion one approved prompt away for 600 people
logging detects misuse only afterwards
a name prefix is a hint, not a control

questions.q: The internal Jira MCP server authenticates every engineer with one shared admin service token. Auditors cannot tell who changed what, and the security team requires each action to run with only that engineer's own Jira permissions. What is the best fix?
options: Have the MCP server use each engineer's own OAuth login, so every action is scoped to and attributed to that user
Add each engineer's name to every request as a header so that the logs show who sent each request
Rotate the shared service token every month so that a leaked copy stops working fairly quickly
Store the shared token in a central secrets manager instead of leaving it in each engineer's local environment
questions.explain: Both requirements, attribution and per-user permissions, are met only if each action runs as the engineer, which delegated OAuth does. The name header is the near-miss: it targets attribution, but it is self-asserted and spoofable, and every request still carries admin rights. Rotation and a secrets manager protect the token better without changing who it lets act or what it lets them do.
questions.constraint: actions must be attributable and run with only that engineer's own permissions
breaks: self-asserted and spoofable, and every request still has admin rights
still one shared admin identity; rotation only shortens the leak window
better storage for a shared admin token, which still gives everyone admin

questions.q: Leadership asks whether Claude Code has actually improved engineering productivity. Which measurement approach is most credible?
options: Lead time and change-failure rate, compared across teams on a staggered rollout
The share of merged lines written by Claude, tracked weekly for each of the 40 teams
The number of Claude Code sessions per engineer per day, as shown by usage analytics
A one-time survey asking engineers how much faster they feel since getting Claude Code
questions.explain: Delivery outcomes such as lead time, with change-failure rate as a quality guard, measure what leadership cares about, and a staggered rollout gives a comparison group so the effect is not confused with other changes. The share of Claude-written lines is the near-miss: it is easy to measure and shows usage, but more generated code is not more value and can even mean more churn. Session counts are adoption, and a one-off survey measures perception.
questions.constraint: leadership wants a credible measure of productivity
breaks: generated lines measure usage, not value
session counts measure adoption
a one-off survey measures perception

questions.q: The company must be able to guarantee to auditors that no AI-assisted change reaches the main branch without human review, whether it was pushed by Claude Code, a script or an engineer with admin rights. Which TWO controls provide that guarantee? Select TWO.
options: A CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude never to push to the main branch without a reviewed and approved pull request
Branch protection that requires an approved pull request before anything can be merged to main
A weekly report of direct pushes to main, with follow-up by the teams involved
Apply the protection rule to administrators and bots too, with direct pushes to main blocked
questions.explain: A guarantee needs a control the system enforces, and it must cover every pusher including administrators and bots. The CLAUDE.md rule is the near-miss: Claude will usually follow it, but it is guidance and does nothing about a script or a person. A weekly report detects violations after they have reached main.
questions.constraint: a guarantee covering Claude, scripts and admins, not an expectation
breaks: guidance to Claude only; does not bind scripts or people
detects violations after they have reached main

questions.q: How should the platform team roll Claude Code out to 40 teams?
options: Enable it for all 40 teams at once so that adoption builds momentum from the start
Pilot only with the most enthusiastic early adopters, then enable it for everyone
Pilot with a few representative teams against agreed metrics, then expand in waves
Wait until every team's concerns are resolved in writing before enabling anyone
questions.explain: A staged rollout with representative pilot teams and agreed success metrics surfaces configuration and workflow problems while they are cheap to fix, and each wave builds on evidence. The enthusiasts-only pilot is the near-miss: piloting is right, but self-selected fans are not representative, so the results overstate the benefit and miss the problems sceptical teams will hit. Big-bang rollout multiplies early mistakes, and waiting for unanimity never ships.
questions.constraint: rolling out to 40 teams
breaks: a big-bang rollout multiplies early mistakes
an enthusiast-only pilot is not representative
waiting for unanimity never ships

questions.q: The CISO is worried about source code leaving the company through Claude Code and wants a written answer before any rollout decision. Anything that does not describe this deployment's own data flows will be challenged. How should you address the concern?
options: Point to the vendor's SOC 2 report, which covers the controls the CISO is most concerned about
Run a live demo so the CISO can see how much faster engineers complete their tasks
Propose starting with engineers' personal accounts, so that the company carries no direct exposure to the code at all
Map each concern to what data is sent, how long it is retained and which control limits it, including residual risk
questions.explain: The CISO asked about specifics, so answer with specifics for this deployment: what is sent, how long it is kept, and which settings, contracts and policies limit it, plus any residual risk. The SOC 2 report is the near-miss: genuine evidence about the vendor's controls, but it says nothing about what this deployment sends or how it is configured. A productivity demo changes the subject, and personal accounts remove the company's controls entirely.
questions.constraint: written answer about this deployment's own data flows
breaks: vendor-level evidence that does not describe this deployment's data flows
changes the subject from risk to speed
removes the company's controls entirely

questions.q: Forty teams now send requests to change the shared Claude Code setup. How should the platform team manage this feedback loop?
options: Run one intake channel, triage requests monthly with team reps and publish a changelog
Let each team edit the shared configuration directly whenever it needs something new
Collect feedback only in the annual engineering survey to avoid overloading the teams
Accept every team's request in the order received, so that nobody feels ignored
questions.explain: A sustainable feedback loop has one place requests land, a regular triage with the people affected, and a visible record of what changed and why. Direct edits are the near-miss: they are fast and responsive, but shared configuration then changes without review and one team's fix can break another's workflow. Annual surveys are too slow, and first-come-first-served ignores impact.
questions.constraint: 40 teams are requesting changes to one shared setup
breaks: unreviewed direct edits let one team's fix break another's workflow
an annual survey is too slow
first come, first served ignores impact

questions.q: Claude translates legal notices that must meet a strict glossary and style checklist. First drafts usually miss a few items, and a reviewer can always say exactly which. Which workflow pattern fits best?
options: Draft, have an evaluator check it against the checklist, and revise until it passes
Generate three drafts in parallel and keep whichever one a judge scores as the best
Give an autonomous agent web search so it can look up glossary terms it is unsure of
Route each notice to a different prompt depending on the language it is going into
questions.explain: When output can be checked against clear criteria and feedback reliably improves it, the evaluator-optimizer pattern fits: one call drafts, another checks against the checklist and names the misses, and the draft is revised within a bounded number of rounds. Parallel drafts with a judge is the near-miss: it picks the best of three, but if every draft misses a few items, choosing the best still ships a failing one, because nothing feeds the specific misses back. Web search does not supply a house glossary, and routing by language does not check anything.
questions.constraint: output is checkable against a checklist and a reviewer can name each miss
breaks: the best of three still ships a failing draft
web search does not supply a house glossary
routing by language checks nothing

questions.q: Under which TWO conditions does a multi-agent design earn its extra cost and complexity? Select TWO.
options: The task sounds sophisticated and stakeholders expect an advanced design
The subtasks need genuinely different tools and context from one another
The steps run in a fixed order and each depends on the last step's output
The subtasks are independent of each other and can usefully run in parallel
questions.explain: Multi-agent designs pay off when subtasks need different tools and context, so separate agents keep each context focused, and when they are independent enough to run in parallel. A fixed sequence of dependent steps is the near-miss: it is genuine decomposition, but it suits a workflow or prompt chain, where code passes each output on, not coordinating agents. Sophistication and stakeholder expectations are not technical reasons.
questions.constraint: when a multi-agent design earns its cost
breaks: sophistication is not a technical reason
a fixed dependent sequence suits a workflow or prompt chain

questions.q: A bank wants Claude to help relationship managers offer same-day credit memos, a service it has never been able to offer. Which business value pillar is primary?
options: Efficiency, because each memo takes relationship managers less time to produce
Transformation, because it enables a service the bank could not offer before
Cost, because each memo needs fewer analyst hours and less paid overtime
Performance SLAs, because memo turnaround is now measured in hours, not days
questions.explain: Transformation is about doing something new, here a service the bank could not provide, and the business case should be framed around the revenue or retention it unlocks. Efficiency is the near-miss: memos may well take less time, but faster production of an existing output is not what this initiative is for, and framing it that way undersells it. Cost and SLAs are secondary effects.
questions.constraint: a service the bank could never offer before
breaks: efficiency undersells a new service as faster production of an existing output
cost savings are a secondary effect
turnaround is a side effect, not the purpose

questions.q: A pipeline classifies 5 million tickets a month into 20 queues. The large model is 97% accurate; the smallest is 95.5% on the same eval at a fraction of the cost. A misrouted ticket is re-queued by staff within minutes. Which choice is best justified?
options: Keep the large model, since a 1.5-point accuracy drop is too much to accept anywhere
Use the large model at night and the small one by day to balance the two costs
Use the small model, since errors are cheap to correct and the cost saving is large
Fine-tune the large model further so it reaches 99% before cost is reconsidered
questions.explain: Model choice weighs the cost of errors against the cost of the model. Here an error costs minutes of staff time, while the price gap across 5 million tickets is large, so the small model wins clearly. Keeping the large model is the near-miss: higher accuracy is genuinely better, and it would be the right call if a misroute were costly or irreversible, but this stem says it is neither. Time-of-day splitting has no basis, and further fine-tuning increases cost to solve a problem that does not need solving.
questions.constraint: a misroute is re-queued within minutes; 5 million tickets a month
breaks: errors are cheap to fix, so 1.5 points are not worth the cost
a time-of-day split has no basis
fine-tuning solves a problem that does not need solving

questions.q: In which workload does prompt caching give the least benefit?
options: A 20,000-token policy manual sent unchanged ahead of thousands of short questions
A long agent conversation where each turn resends the full earlier history unchanged
A large set of tool definitions that stays identical on every request in a session
A unique 30,000-token contract per request, behind a short shared instruction block
questions.explain: Caching reuses an identical prefix, so the benefit depends on how much of each prompt repeats. With a unique contract every time, only the short instruction block can be reused, and it may even fall under the minimum cacheable length. The long agent conversation is the near-miss: it looks like everything changes, but each turn resends the earlier history unchanged as a prefix, which caches well. A static manual and identical tool definitions are the textbook cases.
questions.constraint: caching helps only where the prefix repeats
breaks: a static manual is a textbook cache case
a resent history prefix repeats and caches well
identical tool definitions are a textbook cache case

questions.q: Which TWO situations most favour building an MCP server rather than a direct API integration? Select TWO.
options: Several different Claude applications and clients all need the same capability
A single nightly script calls one endpoint, and nothing else will ever use it
The integration is a one-off data migration that will be deleted once it has run
The owning team wants one maintained interface that every agent can reuse
questions.explain: MCP pays off through reuse: one server, maintained by the team that owns the system, serves every Claude app and client that needs it. The nightly script is the near-miss: MCP would work there, but with one consumer and one endpoint the protocol layer adds a server to run and secure for no reuse benefit, so a direct API call is simpler. A one-off migration is the same case taken further.
questions.constraint: one capability reused by several clients and agents
breaks: one consumer and one endpoint: MCP adds a server for no reuse
a one-off migration deleted afterwards needs no protocol layer

questions.q: After the team switched the LLM judge in their eval pipeline to a new model, every system variant's score rose about 8 points overnight. What should they do first?
options: Average the scores of two different judge models so each one's bias cancels out
Ask the judge to explain each score, since a reasoned score is a trustworthy score
Measure the new judge's agreement with a human-labelled sample before trusting it
Use the largest available model as the judge, since stronger models judge accurately
questions.explain: A uniform jump across all variants after changing only the judge says the ruler moved, not the systems. Before trusting any judge, check its agreement with human labels on a sample, and re-baseline. Averaging two judges is the near-miss: ensembles can reduce noise, but nobody knows whether either judge agrees with humans, so the average inherits unknown bias. Explanations can rationalise any score, and judge size does not guarantee calibration.
questions.constraint: every variant rose about 8 points after only the judge changed
breaks: averaging two judges inherits unknown bias
explanations can rationalise any score
judge size does not guarantee calibration

questions.q: Which TWO statements describe correct placement of controls in a Claude system's safety stack? Select TWO.
options: Output screening of replies removes the need for authorisation on tool calls
Input screening runs before the model call, catching injection and abuse attempts
Tool-call authorisation is checked in the tool layer, whatever the model decided
System-prompt rules are the main control against destructive tool actions
questions.explain: Each layer catches a different failure: input screening stops hostile content before the model reads it, and authorisation in the tool layer means a tool action is allowed or refused by the system, not by the model's judgement. Output screening is the near-miss: it is a real layer, but it inspects what the model says, while a tool call acts on the world before any reply is screened. System-prompt rules guide behaviour but are not a security boundary.
questions.constraint: placing controls in the right layer of the safety stack
breaks: output screening does not replace tool authorisation
system-prompt rules are not a security boundary

questions.q: A European retailer's chat assistant processes customers' names, addresses and order histories. Which regulation and obligations apply most directly?
options: HIPAA, requiring a business associate agreement before customer data is processed
PCI DSS, requiring every chat transcript to be encrypted with keys rotated quarterly
FedRAMP, requiring the assistant to run in an authorised government cloud environment
GDPR, requiring a lawful basis, data minimisation, retention limits and subject rights
questions.explain: Personal data of people in the EU falls under GDPR, which drives lawful basis, minimisation, retention limits and rights such as access and erasure. PCI DSS is the near-miss: retail suggests payments, but it governs cardholder data, and names, addresses and order histories are not card data. HIPAA covers US health information, and FedRAMP covers US federal cloud services.
questions.constraint: a European retailer processing names, addresses and order histories
breaks: HIPAA covers US health information
PCI DSS covers cardholder data, not names and addresses
FedRAMP covers US federal cloud services

questions.q: Months after the team chose retrieval over fine-tuning, new stakeholders keep reopening the question 'why didn't we fine-tune?'. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Re-run the full fine-tuning analysis each time someone raises the question again
Record the decision, alternatives, evidence and a trigger for revisiting it in an ADR
Tell stakeholders the decision is final and that the topic is now closed for good
Agree to fine-tune as well, since doing both avoids having to defend the decision
questions.explain: An architecture decision record captures what was decided, the alternatives weighed, the evidence and the conditions under which the decision should be revisited, so newcomers get the reasoning without a rerun and the team knows when reopening is justified. Re-running the analysis is the near-miss: it treats the question seriously, but repeats work every time and still leaves no durable record. Declaring the topic closed shuts out legitimate new evidence, and doing both doubles cost to avoid a conversation.
questions.constraint: newcomers keep reopening a settled decision
breaks: re-running the analysis repeats work and leaves no record
closing the topic shuts out legitimate new evidence
doing both doubles cost to avoid a conversation
